title: Neem (Azadirachta indica): Uses, Evidence & Safety
metaDescription: Neem (Azadirachta indica): traditional Ayurvedic uses for skin and mouth, what the evidence shows, and serious safety cautions — neem oil toxicity, children and pregnancy.
h1: Neem (Azadirachta indica): Traditional Use, Evidence and Cautions
answerCapsule: Neem (Azadirachta indica), the tree known in Sanskrit as nimba, is used in Ayurveda for the skin, mouth and gut. Laboratory and animal studies have examined it widely, but human evidence for most claimed uses is thin. Neem oil is genuinely dangerous if swallowed, especially by infants, and neem should be avoided in pregnancy.

sections.capsule: Neem (Azadirachta indica), called nimba (IAST: nimba) in Sanskrit and margosa or Indian lilac in English, is a fast-growing evergreen of the mahogany family native to the Indian subcontinent. Ayurveda classes neem as a bitter, cooling herb and has long used its leaf, bark, seed oil and twigs for the skin, mouth and digestion.
sections.body:
Neem is one of the most widely used plants in traditional Indian medicine, valued for its intensely bitter taste. Classical Ayurveda describes it as *tikta* (bitter) and cooling, and traditionally applies neem leaf and oil to the skin and neem twigs to the teeth and gums [1]. In the West it is marketed for acne, dandruff and oral care, and neem oil is a common garden pesticide.

The medicinal parts are not interchangeable. Neem leaf, bark and seed oil differ in chemistry, and neem seed oil in particular concentrates compounds such as azadirachtin that make it useful as a pesticide but hazardous to swallow. Where neem is linked in tradition with cooling an aggravated [pitta or kapha](/doshas), that is a classical framing, not a biomedical one.

sections.h2: What does the science say about neem?
sections.capsule: Neem has been studied mostly in the laboratory and in animals, not in people. Cell and rodent studies report antibacterial, antifungal, anti-ulcer and anti-inflammatory activity, and neem twig chewing has some evidence for dental plaque [1]. Robust human trials for treating any disease are largely absent, so neem is best seen as traditionally used and preliminarily studied, not proven.
sections.body:
Neem's reputation rests far more on tradition and laboratory work than on clinical trials. Test-tube and animal studies have reported a broad range of activities — antibacterial, antifungal, antiviral and anti-inflammatory among them — but a Memorial Sloan Kettering summary notes that neem has *not* been studied as a treatment for cancer in humans, with the anticancer findings confined to cells and animals [1].

The most human-relevant signal is dental. Neem-based mouth rinses and chewing sticks have been reported to reduce dental plaque and oral bacterial counts, though the data are described as conflicting [1]. Beyond oral care, high-quality human trials are scarce, and none establishes neem as a treatment for a diagnosed illness. For how Ayurvedic evidence is weighed more broadly, see [Is Ayurveda scientific?](/is-ayurveda-scientific).

sections.h2: What are the side effects and cautions of neem?
sections.capsule: Neem oil is the real hazard: swallowing even small amounts has caused vomiting, seizures, liver injury and toxic encephalopathy, and case series describe deaths in infants given neem oil [1][3]. Neem should never be given to babies or young children, and it should be avoided in pregnancy because of documented antifertility and anti-implantation effects in animals [5].
sections.body:
The cautions here are unusually serious for a herb, and they centre on neem oil.

- **Neem oil poisoning:** swallowing neem oil can cause vomiting, drowsiness, metabolic acidosis, seizures, liver toxicity and toxic encephalopathy in both children and adults [3]. In infants and small children it is especially dangerous: a single dose has led to severe poisoning, and case reports and series describe brain injury and deaths [1][2]. Neem oil is not a home remedy for babies and must be kept well out of reach.
- **Pregnancy and fertility:** neem seed extracts and neem oil have documented antifertility, spermicidal and anti-implantation effects in animal studies, and reviewers advise partners planning a family to avoid them; on the same basis neem should be avoided in pregnancy [5].
- **Medicine interactions:** a neem extract inhibited the drug-metabolising enzyme CYP3A4 in the laboratory; the clinical relevance is unknown, so tell your doctor if you take regular medication [1].
- **Contamination:** as with any Ayurvedic product, sourcing quality — not the plant alone — drives heavy-metal risk [4].

Topical neem is better tolerated but can cause allergic skin reactions such as rash and itching [1]. None of this is medical advice; anyone on medication, pregnant, or considering neem for a child should speak to a qualified clinician first.

sections.h2: Where can I find quality neem?
sections.capsule: Neem products vary widely in quality, and neem oil in particular carries real toxicity, so sourcing matters more than usual. Choose neem grown and processed under a recognised Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) standard with heavy-metal testing, and never use undiluted neem oil internally. Where neem is used within care, that is under physician supervision at a NABH-accredited Ayurvedic hospital.
sections.body:
Two facts make sourcing especially important for neem. First, neem oil is toxic if swallowed, so it should only ever be used as directed and never given internally to children [1][3]. Second, like all Ayurvedic products, neem preparations can be contaminated with heavy metals such as lead, mercury and arsenic when made without proper controls — a risk documented across the wider market [4].

Prefer neem from a maker that names the plant part, follows a recognised **Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) standard**, and tests for heavy metals. That is a statement about quality control, not a claim that neem treats any condition. If you are considering neem beyond ordinary skin or oral-care use, a qualified Ayurvedic physician can advise whether it suits you, and where it is used clinically that happens inside a full consultation at a NABH-accredited hospital. You can compare neem with other commonly discussed herbs on the [herbs overview](/herbs), including [shatavari](/herbs/shatavari).

faqs.q: Is neem safe to take by mouth?
faqs.a: Neem leaf products are generally tolerated in the short term, but neem oil is genuinely dangerous to swallow — it has caused seizures, liver injury and, in infants, death. Neem should not be taken internally by babies or children, should be avoided in pregnancy, and used only cautiously and briefly by adults, ideally with professional guidance.

faqs.q: Can neem be used during pregnancy?
faqs.a: No. Neem seed extracts and neem oil have shown antifertility, anti-implantation and abortifacient-type effects in animal studies, so neem should be avoided in pregnancy and by anyone actively trying to conceive. If you are pregnant or planning a pregnancy, do not take neem without medical advice.

faqs.q: Does neem help with acne or skin problems?
faqs.a: Neem is traditionally applied to the skin and is a common ingredient in acne and dandruff products, and laboratory studies show antibacterial and antifungal activity. Good human trials are limited, so treat it as a traditional skincare herb with early evidence rather than a proven acne treatment.

faqs.q: Is neem oil the same as neem leaf?
faqs.a: No. Neem leaf, bark and seed oil differ in chemistry. Neem seed oil concentrates compounds like azadirachtin that make it a useful pesticide but hazardous to swallow, which is why most serious poisonings involve neem oil rather than neem leaf. Always check which part a product contains.
